# Chapter I: General Provisions (Articles 1-4)

## Article 1: Subject Matter

1. The purpose of this Regulation is to improve the functioning of the internal market and promote the uptake of human-centric and trustworthy artificial intelligence (AI), while ensuring a high level of protection of health, safety, fundamental rights enshrined in the Charter, including democracy, the rule of law and environmental protection, against the harmful effects of AI systems in the Union and supporting innovation.

2. This Regulation lays down:

(a) harmonised rules for the placing on the market, the putting into service, and the use of AI systems in the Union;

(b) prohibitions of certain AI practices;

(c) specific requirements for high-risk AI systems and obligations for operators of such systems;

(d) harmonised transparency rules for certain AI systems;

(e) harmonised rules for the placing on the market of general-purpose AI models;

(f) rules on market monitoring, market surveillance, governance and enforcement;

(g) measures to support innovation, with a particular focus on SMEs, including startups.

## Article 2: Scope

1. This Regulation applies to:

(a) providers placing on the market or putting into service AI systems or placing on the market general-purpose AI models in the Union, irrespective of whether those providers are established or located within the Union or in a third country;

(b) deployers of AI systems that have their place of establishment or are located within the Union;

(c) providers and deployers of AI systems that have their place of establishment or are located in a third country, where the output produced by the AI system is used in the Union;

(d) importers and distributors of AI systems;

(e) product manufacturers placing on the market or putting into service an AI system together with their product and under their own name or trademark;

(f) authorised representatives of providers, which are not established in the Union;

(g) affected persons that are located in the Union.

8. This Regulation does not apply to any research, testing or development activity regarding AI systems or AI models prior to their being placed on the market or put into service. Such activities shall be conducted in accordance with applicable Union law. Testing in real world conditions shall not be covered by that exclusion.

9. This Regulation is without prejudice to the rules laid down by other Union legal acts related to consumer protection and product safety.

10. This Regulation does not apply to obligations of deployers who are natural persons using AI systems in the course of a purely personal non-professional activity.

11. This Regulation does not preclude the Union or Member States from maintaining or introducing laws, regulations or administrative provisions which are more favourable to workers in terms of protecting their rights in respect of the use of AI systems by employers, or from encouraging or allowing the application of collective agreements which are more favourable to workers.

12. This Regulation does not apply to AI systems released under free and open-source licences, unless they are placed on the market or put into service as high-risk AI systems or as an AI system that falls under Article 5 or 50.

## Article 3: Definitions

For the purposes of this Regulation, the following definitions apply:

(1) 'AI system' means a machine-based system that is designed to operate with varying levels of autonomy and that may exhibit adaptiveness after deployment, and that, for explicit or implicit objectives, infers, from the input it receives, how to generate outputs such as predictions, content, recommendations, or decisions that can influence physical or virtual environments.

(2) 'risk' means the combination of the probability of an occurrence of harm and the severity of that harm.

(3) 'provider' means a natural or legal person, public authority, agency or other body that develops an AI system or a general-purpose AI model or that has an AI system or a general-purpose AI model developed and places it on the market or puts the AI system into service under its own name or trademark, whether for payment or free of charge.

(4) 'deployer' means a natural or legal person, public authority, agency or other body using an AI system under its authority except where the AI system is used in the course of a personal non-professional activity.

(5) 'authorised representative' means a natural or legal person located or established in the Union who has received and accepted a written mandate from a provider of an AI system or a general-purpose AI model to, respectively, perform and carry out on its behalf the obligations and procedures established by this Regulation.

**Article 27: Fundamental Rights Impact Assessment for High-Risk AI Systems**
### Article 27: Fundamental Rights Impact Assessment for High-Risk AI Systems

1. Prior to deploying a high-risk AI system referred to in Article 6(2), with the exception of high-risk AI systems intended to be used in the area listed in point 2 of Annex III, deployers that are bodies governed by public law, or are private entities providing public services, and deployers of high-risk AI systems referred to in points 5 (b) and (c) of Annex III, shall perform an assessment of the impact on fundamental rights that the use of such system may produce. For that purpose, deployers shall perform an assessment consisting of:

(a) a description of the deployer's processes in which the high-risk AI system will be used in line with its intended purpose;

(b) a description of the period of time within which, and the frequency with which, each high-risk AI system is intended to be used;

(c) the categories of natural persons and groups likely to be affected by its use in the specific context;

(d) the specific risks of harm likely to have an impact on the categories of natural persons or groups of persons identified pursuant to point (c) of this paragraph, taking into account the information given by the provider pursuant to Article 13;

(e) a description of the implementation of human oversight measures, according to the instructions for use;

(f) the measures to be taken in the case of the materialisation of those risks, including the arrangements for internal governance and complaint mechanisms.

2. The obligation laid down in paragraph 1 applies to the first use of the high-risk AI system. The deployer may, in similar cases, rely on previously conducted fundamental rights impact assessments or existing impact assessments carried out by provider. If, during the use of the high-risk AI system, the deployer considers that any of the elements listed in paragraph 1 has changed or is no longer up to date, the deployer shall take the necessary steps to update the information.

3. Once the assessment referred to in paragraph 1 of this Article has been performed, the deployer shall notify the market surveillance authority of its results, submitting the filled-out template referred to in paragraph 5 of this Article as part of the notification. In the case referred to in Article 46(1), deployers may be exempt from that obligation to notify.

4. If any of the obligations laid down in this Article is already met through the data protection impact assessment conducted pursuant to Article 35 of Regulation (EU) 2016/679 or Article 27 of Directive (EU) 2016/680, the fundamental rights impact assessment referred to in paragraph 1 of this Article shall complement that data protection impact assessment.

**Article 8: Compliance with the Requirements**
### Article 8: Compliance with the Requirements

1. High-risk AI systems shall comply with the requirements laid down in this Section, taking into account their intended purpose as well as the generally acknowledged state of the art on AI and AI-related technologies. The risk management system referred to in Article 9 shall be taken into account when ensuring compliance with those requirements.

2. Where a product contains an AI system, to which the requirements of this Regulation as well as requirements of the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Section A of Annex I apply, providers shall be responsible for ensuring that their product is fully compliant with all applicable requirements under applicable Union harmonisation legislation. In ensuring the compliance of high-risk AI systems referred to in paragraph 1 with the requirements set out in this Section, and in order to ensure consistency, avoid duplication and minimise additional burdens, providers shall have a choice of integrating, as appropriate, the necessary testing and reporting processes, information and documentation they provide with regard to their product into documentation and procedures that already exist and are required under the Union harmonisation legislation listed in Section A of Annex I.

**Article 72: Post-Market Monitoring by Providers and Post-Market Monitoring Plan for High-Risk AI Systems**
### Article 72: Post-Market Monitoring by Providers and Post-Market Monitoring Plan for High-Risk AI Systems

1. Providers shall establish and document a post-market monitoring system in a manner that is proportionate to the nature of the AI technologies and the risks of the high-risk AI system.

2. The post-market monitoring system shall actively and systematically collect, document and analyse relevant data which may be provided by deployers or which may be collected through other sources on the performance of high-risk AI systems throughout their lifetime, and which allow the provider to evaluate the continuous compliance of AI systems with the requirements set out in Chapter III, Section 2. Where relevant, post-market monitoring shall include an analysis of the interaction with other AI systems. This obligation shall not cover sensitive operational data of deployers which are law enforcement authorities.

3. The post-market monitoring system shall be based on a post-market monitoring plan. The post-market monitoring plan shall be part of the technical documentation referred to in Annex IV. The Commission shall adopt an implementing act laying down detailed provisions establishing a template for the post-market monitoring plan and the list of elements to be included in the plan by 2 February 2026. That implementing act shall be adopted in accordance with the examination procedure referred to in Article 98(2).

question.question: Compare NIST AI RMF's MANAGE function with SR 11-7's expectations on model risk treatment and remediation.
question.expected_answer: NIST AI RMF MANAGE (sub-categories MANAGE 1–4) covers risk prioritisation, risk response, response monitoring, and continual improvement — emphasising risk tolerance from GOVERN, residual-risk evaluation, and feedback loops. SR 11-7 treats model risk remediation as part of validation and ongoing monitoring: findings from validation/monitoring must be tracked, prioritised by risk tier, assigned to model owners with remediation deadlines, and escalated to senior management. Both expect risk-tier-driven prioritisation and named owners. SR 11-7 is more prescriptive on escalation (board reporting); MANAGE is more comprehensive on continual improvement and stakeholder feedback.

Below is a side-by-side comparison of **NIST AI RMF 1.0’s MANAGE function** and **SR 11-7 supervisory expectations** for **model risk treatment and remediation**.

| Topic | NIST AI RMF — MANAGE | SR 11-7 — model risk treatment/remediation |
|---|---|---|
| Core purpose | The MANAGE function turns risk analysis from MAP and MEASURE into action: AI risks are “prioritized, responded to, and managed.” **MANAGE 1** requires determining whether the AI system should proceed, prioritizing treatment, planning/documenting responses, and documenting residual risk. *(NIST AI RMF 1.0, §5.4 / Table 4, MANAGE 1.1–1.4).* | SR 11-7 frames model risk as the potential for adverse financial consequences from decisions based on model output, and expects active, appropriate model risk management tailored to the model’s risk profile and the banking organization’s size and complexity. *(SR 11-7, §§I, III, IV).* |
| Risk treatment options | NIST is explicit about risk response choices: responses for high-priority AI risks may include **mitigating, transferring, avoiding, or accepting** risk. *(NIST AI RMF 1.0, §5.4 / Table 4, MANAGE 1.3).* | SR 11-7 is less taxonomy-driven; it expects model risk to be reduced through development controls, validation, ongoing monitoring, outcome analysis, effective challenge, documentation, and governance practices appropriate to the model’s risk. *(SR 11-7, §§III–VII).* |
| Prioritization standard | NIST requires treatment of documented AI risks to be prioritized based on **impact, likelihood, and available resources or methods**. *(NIST AI RMF 1.0, §5.4 / Table 4, MANAGE 1.2).* It also states that highest-risk AI systems call for the most urgent prioritization and most thorough risk management. *(NIST AI RMF 1.0, §1.2.3).* | SR 11-7 expects a risk-based approach: model risk depends on inherent risk, exposure, purpose, and use, and model risk management rigor should be commensurate with those risks and the organization’s complexity. *(SR 11-7, §§III, IV).* |
| Go / no-go and stopping use | NIST expressly requires a determination of whether the AI system achieves its intended purpose and whether development or deployment should proceed. *(NIST AI RMF 1.0, §5.4 / Table 4, MANAGE 1.1).* NIST also states that if an AI system presents unacceptable negative risk—such as imminent severe harm or catastrophic risk—development and deployment should cease safely until risks are sufficiently managed. *(NIST AI RMF 1.0, §1.2.3).* | SR 11-7 expects model use to be aligned with model purpose, business use, and policy, and expects effective challenge by objective experts with standing to effect appropriate changes throughout the model lifecycle. *(SR 11-7, §§IV, III).* SR 11-7 does not express its remediation framework in the same “go/no-go/deactivate” language as NIST, but its validation, monitoring, and effective challenge expectations support restricting, adjusting, or remediating models that are not fit for purpose. *(SR 11-7, §§III, IV, VII).* |
| Remediation mechanics | NIST requires documented plans for high-priority risk responses. *(NIST AI RMF 1.0, §5.4 / Table 4, MANAGE 1.3).* It also requires procedures to respond to and recover from previously unknown risks when identified. *(NIST AI RMF 1.0, §5.4 / Table 4, MANAGE 2.3).* | SR 11-7 emphasizes documentation as a remediation control: documentation should support tracking recommendations, responses, and exceptions and help manage model remediation efforts. *(SR 11-7, §VI, Documentation).* |
| Residual risk | NIST specifically requires documentation of negative residual risks to downstream acquirers and end users. *(NIST AI RMF 1.0, §5.4 / Table 4, MANAGE 1.4).* It defines residual risk as risk remaining after treatment and notes that residual risk directly affects end users or affected individuals and communities. *(NIST AI RMF 1.0, §1.2.4).* | SR 11-7 focuses less on external disclosure of residual risk and more on internal understanding and control of model risk at both individual and aggregate levels. *(SR 11-7, §§III, VI).* It states that aggregate model risk reflects interactions, dependencies, common assumptions, data, methodologies, and other factors that could affect multiple models simultaneously. *(SR 11-7, §III).* |
| Monitoring and post-deployment remediation | NIST treats risk management as continuous and iterative across the AI lifecycle. *(NIST AI RMF 1.0, §5 Core).* It also requires mechanisms to sustain the value of deployed AI systems and mechanisms to supersede, disengage, or deactivate AI systems whose performance or outcomes are inconsistent with intended use. *(NIST AI RMF 1.0, §5.4 / Table 4, MANAGE 2.2, 2.4).* | SR 11-7 expects ongoing monitoring and outcome analysis, including for vendor models, to assess whether models remain accurate, fit for purpose, and reliable. *(SR 11-7, §VII).* SR 11-7’s remediation posture is therefore grounded in validation findings, ongoing monitoring, outcome analysis, and documented follow-up. *(SR 11-7, §§VI–VII).* |
| Third-party/vendor risk treatment | NIST requires AI risks and benefits from third-party resources to be regularly monitored and for risk controls to be applied and documented. *(NIST AI RMF 1.0, §5.4 / Table 4, MANAGE 3.1).* It also requires pre-trained models used for development to be monitored as part of regular monitoring and maintenance. *(NIST AI RMF 1.0, §5.4 / Table 4, MANAGE 3.2).* | SR 11-7 states that vendor and third-party products present unique validation challenges, especially where code, data, or methodology are proprietary, but the principles of model risk management still apply. *(SR 11-7, §VII).* It expects an understanding of the vendor model’s conceptual soundness, design, development data, and performance, plus ongoing monitoring and outcome analysis. *(SR 11-7, §VII).* |
| Governance and accountability | NIST’s MANAGE function is supported by GOVERN requirements for documented roles and responsibilities, ongoing review, AI inventory, and executive responsibility for development/deployment risk decisions. *(NIST AI RMF 1.0, §5.1 / Table 1, GOVERN 1.5–1.7, 2.1–2.3).* | SR 11-7 emphasizes “effective challenge” by objective experts with expertise, independence, and organizational standing to effect changes. *(SR 11-7, §III).* It also expects model risk management practices to be tailored to the banking organization’s model risk profile and operational complexity. *(SR 11-7, §§II–IV).* |
| Scope difference | NIST AI RMF applies broadly to AI systems and socio-technical AI risks across the AI lifecycle. *(NIST AI RMF 1.0, §§2, 5 Core).* | The current SR 11-7 guidance is banking-sector supervisory guidance for models used by banking organizations, especially larger organizations, and defines “model” as a complex quantitative method, system, or approach applying statistical, economic, or financial theories to input data to produce quantitative estimates. *(SR 11-7, §§II–III).* The retrieved current SR 11-7 text states that generative AI and agentic AI are outside its scope, though governance and controls should guide tools not covered and the principles apply to traditional statistical/quantitative and non-generative, non-agentic AI models. *(SR 11-7, §III n.3).* |

### Bottom line

**NIST AI RMF MANAGE is a broad AI risk treatment function**: it emphasizes prioritization, documented response options, residual risk transparency, go/no-go decisions, recovery from unknown risks, third-party AI controls, and deactivation when outcomes are inconsistent with intended use. *(NIST AI RMF 1.0, §5.4 / Table 4, MANAGE 1.1–3.2; §1.2.3; §1.2.4).*

**SR 11-7 is a banking model risk management framework**: it treats remediation as part of a lifecycle of sound development, validation, effective challenge, ongoing monitoring, outcome analysis, documentation, and governance, with rigor scaled to model risk and organizational complexity. *(SR 11-7, §§III–VII).*

In practical terms: **NIST tells an organization how to decide and document what to do with AI risk**, including whether to accept, mitigate, transfer, avoid, pause, or deactivate; **SR 11-7 tells a banking organization how to ensure model weaknesses are identified, challenged, tracked, and remediated through model risk management controls**. *(NIST AI RMF 1.0, §5.4 / Table 4; SR 11-7, §§III, VI–VII).*

I. INTRODUCTION 
Use of models within the banking and financial services industries continues to grow in 
complexity and scope. Advances in technology along with increased competition have driven 
banking organizations to leverage innovative approaches to improve efficiencies, better mitigate 
risks, and help maximize profits. Continued use of models is essential to maintaining the 
competitiveness of banking organizations in the financial system. 
Use of models also can present substantial risk. Such risk, generally referred to as “model 
risk” for purposes of this guidance, can lead to financial loss, errors in financial statements and 
reporting, and flawed financial and risk management decisions, among other types of risk events. 
Model risk can be mitigated through active and appropriate risk management, recognizing that 
the relevance of model risk depends on the nature, scale, and use of the models in relation to the 
associated business risks.  
This guidance highlights sound principles for effective model risk management. As 
reflected in this guidance, model risk management practices vary from banking organization to 
banking organization. Each banking organization ultimately is responsible for adopting model 
risk management practices that are appropriate and effective for managing the specific risks the 
banking organization faces or is likely to face.

5  
Sound practice involves assessing model risk both individually and in aggregate. 
Aggregate risk reflects interactions and dependencies among models; reliance on common 
assumptions, data, or methodologies; and any other factors that could adversely affect several 
models and their outputs simultaneously.   
Sound model risk management also involves “effective challenge,” which refers to the 
critical analysis conducted by objective experts who evaluate model risk and effect appropriate 
changes throughout the model lifecycle, from model development to ongoing monitoring. 
Effective challenge is performed by individuals with the appropriate expertise to conduct a 
critical and objective challenge, sufficient independence to maintain objectivity, as well as the 
organizational standing and influence to effect any change. 
The size and complexity of the banking organization’s operations also may influence the 
range of model risk management. A banking organization with simple operations may not 
conduct model risk management with the same rigor as an organization with relatively more 
complex operations. Furthermore, a banking organization may tailor portions of its model risk 
management practices that are relevant to the risks posed by a particular model and with a level 
of rigor commensurate with that risk. Effective model risk management therefore warrants 
consideration of model risk in the context of the broader business risks that models support or 
influence.

Model Development 
Sound model development activities are aligned with model purpose, business use, and 
banking organization policy. Model development is not purely a technical exercise. The 
developer’s judgment influences the model’s conceptual design and soundness, inputs,

different banking organizations may present different risks. As such, practices that are 
appropriate and effective for one banking organization may be inappropriate and ineffective for a 
banking organization with a different risk profile or that uses a model for a different purpose. 
Although this guidance may be useful for any type of model, the general expectation is 
that it will be most useful for models supporting a banking organization’s significant business 
lines, operations, services, and functions. This guidance does not set forth enforceable standards 
or prescriptive requirements; accordingly, non-compliance with this guidance will not result in 
supervisory criticism against a banking organization.1

Based on supervisory experience and industry feedback, as well as technological 
advancements in modeling over the past several years, the Office of the Comptroller of the 
Currency, Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System, and Federal Deposit Insurance 
Corporation (the “agencies”) are issuing this revised model risk management guidance to clarify 
model risk management principles, and to set forth a risk-based approach to model risk 
management, tailored to a banking organization’s model risk profile and the size and complexity 
of its operations. 
This guidance is expected to be most relevant to banking organizations with over $30 
billion in total assets.2 Models used by banking organizations with total assets of $30 billion or

It is common industry practice for banking organizations to maintain a comprehensive set

management. While the inventory may contain varying levels of information to reflect different

The widespread use of customized vendor and other third-party products—including

proprietary, banking organizations may not receive from the vendor the underlying code, data, or

principles of model risk management remain applicable.

either by internal or outside parties. Sound practice includes developing an understanding of the

vendor model, including its conceptual soundness, design, development data, and performance.

question.question: How do GDPR (Recital 26 + Article 4(5)) and HIPAA (§164.514) each define and treat 'de-identification' of personal data? Cite the standards each accepts.
question.expected_answer: GDPR Recital 26 + Article 4(5) define anonymous information as data not relating to an identified or identifiable natural person — once truly anonymous, GDPR no longer applies. Pseudonymisation (Art 4(5)) reduces but does not eliminate identifiability — pseudonymised data is still personal data. There is no single statutory standard; the test is whether re-identification is reasonably likely considering all means likely to be used. HIPAA §164.514(b) accepts two standards: (1) Safe Harbor — removal of 18 specified identifiers AND no actual knowledge that the residual data could be used alone or in combination to identify; (2) Expert Determination — a qualified expert determines the risk is very small and documents the methods. HIPAA's standard is procedurally defined; GDPR's is principle-based and stricter (no realistic re-identification risk).

Below is the core distinction:

| Framework | Concept closest to “de-identification” | When data is treated as outside privacy-regime scope | Accepted standard / method |
|---|---|---|---|
| **GDPR** | **Anonymisation**; **pseudonymisation** is separately defined | Only when data is anonymous so the person is **not or no longer identifiable** | A contextual identifiability test considering “all means reasonably likely” to identify the person; no fixed safe-harbor list in Recital 26 / Article 4(5) |
| **HIPAA** | **De-identification of protected health information** | When health information does not identify an individual and there is **no reasonable basis** to believe it can be used to identify the individual | Either **Expert Determination** or **Safe Harbor** removal of specified identifiers |

## GDPR: anonymisation vs. pseudonymisation

### 1. Anonymous data is outside GDPR, but the threshold is contextual  
GDPR Recital 26 says the GDPR’s data-protection principles do **not** apply to “anonymous information,” meaning information that does not relate to an identified or identifiable natural person, or personal data rendered anonymous so that the data subject is **not or no longer identifiable**. It also says identifiability must be assessed by considering **all means reasonably likely to be used**, such as singling out, by the controller or another person, taking into account objective factors such as cost, time, available technology, and technological developments. **Citation: GDPR Recital 26.**

### 2. Pseudonymisation is not full anonymisation  
GDPR Article 4(5) defines **pseudonymisation** as processing personal data so that it can no longer be attributed to a specific data subject **without additional information**, provided that the additional information is kept separately and protected by technical and organisational measures to prevent attribution to an identified or identifiable person. **Citation: GDPR Article 4(5).**

Recital 26 further treats pseudonymised data as still potentially **personal data** if it can be attributed to a natural person through additional information. **Citation: GDPR Recital 26.**

### GDPR accepted “standard”  
GDPR does **not** provide a HIPAA-style list of identifiers whose removal automatically qualifies data as anonymous in Recital 26 or Article 4(5). Instead, it accepts an **anonymisation standard based on whether re-identification is reasonably likely**, considering means available to the controller or others and objective factors such as cost, time, technology, and technological development. **Citation: GDPR Recital 26.**  
For pseudonymisation, the accepted standard is separation of the re-identification information plus technical and organisational controls preventing attribution. **Citation: GDPR Article 4(5).**

## HIPAA: de-identification of PHI

### 1. De-identified health information is not individually identifiable health information  
HIPAA provides that health information is not individually identifiable health information if it does **not identify an individual** and there is **no reasonable basis** to believe it can be used to identify an individual. **Citation: 45 C.F.R. § 164.514(a).**

### 2. HIPAA accepts two de-identification methods

#### A. Expert Determination method  
A covered entity may determine information is not individually identifiable if a person with appropriate knowledge and experience with generally accepted statistical and scientific principles determines that the risk is **very small** that the information could be used, alone or with other reasonably available information, by an anticipated recipient to identify the individual, and documents the methods and results supporting that determination. **Citation: 45 C.F.R. § 164.514(b)(1).**

#### B. Safe Harbor method  
Alternatively, HIPAA permits de-identification by removing specified identifiers of the individual and of relatives, employers, or household members, and having no actual knowledge that the remaining information could identify the individual. **Citation: 45 C.F.R. § 164.514(b)(2).**

The Safe Harbor identifiers include: names; geographic subdivisions smaller than a state subject to limited ZIP-code rules; dates except year and ages over 89 except as “90 or older”; telephone numbers; fax numbers; email addresses; Social Security numbers; medical record numbers; health plan beneficiary numbers; account numbers; certificate/license numbers; vehicle identifiers; device identifiers; URLs; IP addresses; biometric identifiers; full-face photos and comparable images; and any other unique identifying number, characteristic, or code, subject to the re-identification code rule. **Citation: 45 C.F.R. § 164.514(b)(2)(i).**

### 3. Re-identification codes are allowed only under constraints  
HIPAA allows a covered entity to assign a code or other record-identification mechanism to permit re-identification, but the code must not be derived from or related to information about the individual and must not be capable of translation to identify the individual; the covered entity also must not use or disclose the mechanism for re-identification. **Citation: 45 C.F.R. § 164.514(c).**

## Bottom line

- **GDPR** treats true anonymisation as outside GDPR, but uses a **risk/context-based identifiability test**; **pseudonymisation is still personal data** if re-identification is possible with additional information. **Citations: GDPR Recital 26; GDPR Article 4(5).**
- **HIPAA** expressly defines de-identification and accepts two concrete standards: **Expert Determination** and **Safe Harbor** removal of enumerated identifiers plus no actual knowledge of identifiability. **Citations: 45 C.F.R. § 164.514(a), (b)(1), (b)(2).**

### Article 4 — Definitions

For the purposes of this Regulation:

‘restriction of processing’ means the marking of stored personal data with the aim of limiting their processing in the future;

‘profiling’ means any form of automated processing of personal data consisting of the use of personal data to evaluate certain personal aspects relating to a natural person, in particular to analyse or predict aspects concerning that natural person’s performance at work, economic situation, health, personal preferences, interests, reliability, behaviour, location or movements;

‘pseudonymisation’ means the processing of personal data in such a manner that the personal data can no longer be attributed to a specific data subject without the use of additional information, provided that such additional information is kept separately and is subject to technical and organisational measures to ensure that the personal data are not attributed to an identified or identifiable natural person;

‘filing system’ means any structured set of personal data which are accessible according to specific criteria, whether centralised, decentralised or dispersed on a functional or geographical basis;

**Article 11 — Processing which does not require identification**
### Article 11 — Processing which does not require identification

If the purposes for which a controller processes personal data do not or do no longer require the identification of a data subject by the controller, the controller shall not be obliged to maintain, acquire or process additional information in order to identify the data subject for the sole purpose of complying with this Regulation.

1Where, in cases referred to in paragraph 1 of this Article, the controller is able to demonstrate that it is not in a position to identify the data subject, the controller shall inform the data subject accordingly, if possible. 2In such cases, Articles 15 to 20 shall not apply except where the data subject, for the purpose of exercising his or her rights under those articles, provides additional information enabling his or her identification.


## Chapter III: Rights of the Data Subject

**Article 25 — Data protection by design and by default**
### Article 25 — Data protection by design and by default

Taking into account the state of the art, the cost of implementation and the nature, scope, context and purposes of processing as well as the risks of varying likelihood and severity for rights and freedoms of natural persons posed by the processing, the controller shall, both at the time of the determination of the means for processing and at the time of the processing itself, implement appropriate technical and organisational measures, such as pseudonymisation, which are designed to implement data-protection principles, such as data minimisation, in an effective manner and to integrate the necessary safeguards into the processing in order to meet the requirements of this Regulation and protect the rights of data subjects.

1The controller shall implement appropriate technical and organisational measures for ensuring that, by default, only personal data which are necessary for each specific purpose of the processing are processed. 2That obligation applies to the amount of personal data collected, the extent of their processing, the period of their storage and their accessibility. 3In particular, such measures shall ensure that by default personal data are not made accessible without the individual’s intervention to an indefinite number of natural persons.

the pseudonymisation and encryption of personal data;

This Regulation lays down rules relating to the protection of natural persons with regard to the processing of personal data and rules relating to the free movement of personal data.

question.question: Compare SOC 2 CC7.4 (security incident response) with GDPR Article 33 (notification to supervisory authority) on incident-response obligations.
question.expected_answer: SOC 2 CC7.4 requires the entity to respond to identified security events by executing a defined incident-response programme to understand, contain, remediate, and communicate security incidents. Specific elements: incident-response plan, defined roles, communication procedures, root-cause analysis, and post-incident review. GDPR Article 33 imposes a specific external obligation: notification to the supervisory authority within 72 hours of becoming aware of a personal data breach (unless unlikely to result in risk to data subjects), including specified content (nature of breach, categories/numbers affected, contact, likely consequences, measures taken). SOC 2 covers internal handling; GDPR adds an external regulatory clock and content requirements specifically for *personal data* breaches.
question.notes: Internal incident response vs external regulatory notification.

output.answer:
Below is a focused comparison of **SOC 2 CC7.4** and **GDPR Article 33** on incident-response obligations.

| Topic | SOC 2 CC7.4 | GDPR Article 33 |
|---|---|---|
| Core obligation | Requires the entity to **respond to identified security incidents** by executing a **defined incident-response program** to “understand, contain, remediate, and communicate” incidents as appropriate. **(SOC 2, CC7.4)** | Requires a **controller** to notify the competent supervisory authority of a **personal data breach** without undue delay and, where feasible, within **72 hours** after becoming aware of it, unless the breach is unlikely to result in risk to individuals’ rights and freedoms. **(GDPR, Art. 33(1))** |
| Trigger | Triggered by an **identified security incident** requiring management action to protect information assets/resources. **(SOC 2, definitions of “security incident”; SOC 2, CC7.4)** | Triggered by a **personal data breach**, defined as a security breach leading to accidental or unlawful destruction, loss, alteration, unauthorized disclosure of, or access to personal data. **(GDPR, Art. 4 definition of “personal data breach”; GDPR, Art. 33(1))** |
| Scope | Broader security-operations control covering incident-response governance, containment, remediation, restoration, communications, and program effectiveness. **(SOC 2, CC7.4 points of focus)** | Narrower legal notification duty focused on reporting qualifying **personal data breaches** to the supervisory authority. **(GDPR, Art. 33)** |
| Timing | Requires communication protocols for timely communication of security incidents and actions taken, but does **not** prescribe a fixed deadline in CC7.4. **(SOC 2, CC7.4 point of focus: “Develops and Implements Communication of Security Incidents”)** | Requires notification without undue delay and, where feasible, no later than **72 hours** after awareness; late notification must include reasons for the delay. **(GDPR, Art. 33(1))** |
| Responsible parties | Requires assigned roles and responsibilities for the design, implementation, maintenance, and execution of the incident-response program, including use of external resources when necessary. **(SOC 2, CC7.4 point of focus: “Assigns Roles and Responsibilities”)** | Places notification duty on the **controller**; a **processor** must notify the controller without undue delay after becoming aware of a personal data breach. **(GDPR, Art. 33(1)–(2))** |
| Required response activities | Requires procedures to contain, mitigate, resolve incidents, remediate vulnerabilities, restore data and business operations, and evaluate incident-response effectiveness periodically. **(SOC 2, CC7.4 points of focus)** | Requires the notification to describe the breach, affected categories and approximate numbers of data subjects and records where possible, DPO/contact details, likely consequences, and measures taken or proposed to address and mitigate the breach. **(GDPR, Art. 33(3))** |
| Documentation | Requires remediation activities to be documented and communicated under the incident-response program. **(SOC 2, CC7.4 point of focus: “Communicates Remediation Activities”)** | Requires the controller to document any personal data breaches, including facts, effects, and remedial action, so the supervisory authority can verify compliance. **(GDPR, Art. 33(5))** |
| Communication audience | Requires protocols for timely communication to **affected parties** regarding security incidents and actions taken, as appropriate to support entity objectives. **(SOC 2, CC7.4 point of focus: “Develops and Implements Communication of Security Incidents”)** | Requires notification to the **competent supervisory authority**; separate communication to affected individuals is addressed under GDPR Article 34 when the breach is likely to result in high risk. **(GDPR, Art. 33(1); GDPR, Art. 34(1))** |
| Flexibility | Allows the entity to determine appropriate response time frames and containment strategy based on the nature and severity of the incident. **(SOC 2, CC7.4 point of focus: “Obtains Understanding of Nature of Incident and Determines Containment Strategy”)** | Allows phased reporting if all required information cannot be provided at the same time, but the remaining information must be provided without undue further delay. **(GDPR, Art. 33(4))** |

### Key takeaways

1. **SOC 2 CC7.4 is an operational control criterion; GDPR Article 33 is a legal breach-notification obligation.** SOC 2 CC7.4 expects a defined incident-response program covering roles, containment, mitigation, remediation, restoration, communication, and effectiveness evaluation. **(SOC 2, CC7.4)** GDPR Article 33 imposes a specific regulatory notification duty for personal data breaches. **(GDPR, Art. 33)**

2. **GDPR Article 33 is more prescriptive on timing and notification content.** It sets a 72-hour benchmark, requires reasons for delay, and specifies the minimum content of the notification. **(GDPR, Art. 33(1), 33(3))** SOC 2 CC7.4 requires timely communication and response procedures but does not define a fixed notification deadline. **(SOC 2, CC7.4)**

3. **SOC 2 CC7.4 is broader in incident lifecycle coverage.** It covers understanding the incident, containment, mitigation, resolution, vulnerability remediation, restoration of operations, communications, and periodic evaluation of response effectiveness. **(SOC 2, CC7.4 points of focus)** GDPR Article 33 focuses on notification and documentation of personal data breaches, though it also requires describing measures taken or proposed to address and mitigate the breach. **(GDPR, Art. 33(3), 33(5))**

4. **A SOC 2-aligned incident-response program can support GDPR Article 33 compliance, but it is not sufficient by itself.** To satisfy GDPR Article 33, the program must specifically include personal-data-breach assessment, controller/processor escalation paths, 72-hour supervisory-authority notification workflow, required notification content, phased-update procedures, and breach documentation sufficient for supervisory-authority review. **(SOC 2, CC7.4; GDPR, Art. 33(1)–(5))**

question.question: How do EU AI Act Article 14 (human oversight) and SR 11-7's 'effective challenge' principle each ensure that automated/model decisions remain subject to human review?
question.expected_answer: EU AI Act Article 14 requires high-risk AI systems to be designed and developed in a way that natural persons can effectively oversee them during the period in which the system is in use. Specific measures: appropriate human-machine interface tools, ability to interpret outputs, ability to override or refuse to use the system, ability to interrupt operation via a 'stop' button, awareness of automation bias, and competence/authority/training of oversight personnel. SR 11-7's effective challenge is an organisational principle: critical analysis of models by objective, informed parties — qualified people who are independent from development and whose review can effect change. EU AI Act is product-design focused (user-facing oversight controls); SR 11-7 is governance focused (organisational independence and authority).

output.answer:
EU AI Act Article 14 and SR 11-7 both prevent model/AI outputs from becoming unquestioned automated decisions, but they do it at different control layers.

| Framework | Mechanism for human review | What the human must be able to do | Main difference |
|---|---|---|---|
| **EU AI Act, Article 14 — Human Oversight** | Requires **high-risk AI systems** to be designed and developed so they can be **effectively overseen by natural persons while in use**. | Humans assigned oversight must be able to understand the system’s capacities and limits, monitor operation, detect anomalies, avoid automation bias, interpret outputs, disregard/override/reverse outputs, and intervene or stop the system safely. | It is an **operational, use-time safeguard**: the human overseer can review and override particular AI outputs or decisions. |
| **SR 11-7 — Effective Challenge** | Requires model risk management to include **critical analysis by objective experts** who evaluate model risk and require changes across the model lifecycle, from development through ongoing monitoring. | Challengers must have expertise, independence, objectivity, and organizational standing/influence to effect change. | It is a **governance and lifecycle review safeguard**: humans independently challenge the model, its assumptions, use, monitoring, and outputs, but SR 11-7 does not necessarily require human approval of every individual model-driven decision. |

Under the **EU AI Act**, Article 14 is explicit that high-risk AI systems must be capable of human oversight “during the period in which they are in use” and must include appropriate human-machine interface tools (**EU AI Act, Art. 14(1)**). The purpose of that oversight is to prevent or minimize risks to health, safety, or fundamental rights that may arise from intended use or reasonably foreseeable misuse (**EU AI Act, Art. 14(2)**). The Act then operationalizes review by requiring oversight measures proportionate to the system’s risk, autonomy, and context of use (**EU AI Act, Art. 14(3)**), and by enabling human overseers to monitor performance, detect anomalies, understand limitations, avoid automation bias, interpret outputs, disregard or override outputs, reverse outputs, and stop the system safely (**EU AI Act, Art. 14(4)(a)–(e)**). For certain high-risk identification systems listed in Annex III point 1(a), Article 14 goes further: no deployer action or decision may be taken based on the system’s identification unless it is separately verified and confirmed by at least two competent, trained, authorized natural persons, subject to specified exceptions (**EU AI Act, Art. 14(5)**).

Under **SR 11-7**, the human-review concept is framed as **“effective challenge.”** SR 11-7 defines model risk as risk that can arise from decisions made based on model output (**SR 11-7, Section III, Overview of Model Risk and Model Risk Management**). To control that risk, sound model risk management includes effective challenge: critical analysis by objective experts who evaluate model risk and effect appropriate changes throughout the model lifecycle, from model development to ongoing monitoring (**SR 11-7, Section III, Overview of Model Risk and Model Risk Management**). SR 11-7 requires the challengers to have appropriate expertise, independence to maintain objectivity, and sufficient organizational standing and influence to cause changes where needed (**SR 11-7, Section III, Overview of Model Risk and Model Risk Management**). For third-party/vendor models, SR 11-7 also expects validation, ongoing monitoring, outcome analysis, and assessment of whether models remain accurate, fit for purpose, and reliable; such analysis can support overlays or adjustments to model output (**SR 11-7, Section VII, Vendor and Other Third-Party Products**).

In short: **Article 14 makes human oversight a built-in, operational requirement for high-risk AI use, including the ability to override or stop outputs. SR 11-7 makes human review an independent governance discipline, ensuring models and model-based decisions are subject to expert challenge, validation, monitoring, and remediation.**

### Article 14: Human Oversight

1. High-risk AI systems shall be designed and developed in such a way, including with appropriate human-machine interface tools, that they can be effectively overseen by natural persons during the period in which they are in use.

4. For the purpose of implementing paragraphs 1, 2 and 3, the high-risk AI system shall be provided to the deployer in such a way that natural persons to whom human oversight is assigned are enabled, as appropriate and proportionate:

question.question: How does GDPR Article 22 (automated decision-making) interact with the EU AI Act's classification of certain AI systems as high-risk? Are there cases where Article 22 applies but the AI Act does not, or vice versa?
question.expected_answer: GDPR Article 22 applies to decisions based solely on automated processing — including profiling — that produce legal or similarly significant effects on a data subject. The EU AI Act classifies certain AI systems as high-risk based on Annex III categories (e.g. employment, creditworthiness, education) regardless of whether decisions are 'solely' automated. Overlap: automated credit scoring, automated hiring, automated benefit eligibility — both regimes typically apply. Article 22 applies but the AI Act may not: a fully-automated, legally-significant decision using a rules-engine that doesn't meet the AI Act's definition of an AI system (Article 3) or isn't in an Annex III use case. AI Act applies but Article 22 may not: an Annex III high-risk AI that supports rather than makes the decision, leaving a human in the loop (no longer 'solely automated' under Art 22). Both regimes can apply concurrently and create overlapping obligations (right to explanation, human review, fairness/bias controls).

output.answer:
GDPR Article 22 and the EU AI Act are **cumulative but different regimes**. The AI Act expressly says EU personal-data law continues to apply and that the AI Act “shall not affect” GDPR, subject only to specific AI Act provisions such as Articles 10(5) and 59. **EU AI Act Article 2(7).**

## 1) Different triggers

### GDPR Article 22
GDPR Article 22 is triggered where a data subject is subject to a **decision based solely on automated processing, including profiling**, that produces **legal effects** or **similarly significantly affects** them. **GDPR Article 22(1).**

If Article 22 applies, the decision is generally restricted unless it is: necessary for a contract, authorised by Union or Member State law with safeguards, or based on explicit consent. **GDPR Article 22(2).** For contract/explicit-consent cases, the controller must provide safeguards including at least human intervention, the ability to express a view, and the ability to contest the decision. **GDPR Article 22(3).** Special-category data cannot be used for such decisions unless Article 9(2)(a) or 9(2)(g) applies and suitable safeguards are in place. **GDPR Article 22(4).**

### EU AI Act high-risk classification
The AI Act is triggered by whether the system is an **“AI system”**—a machine-based system that operates with varying autonomy and generates outputs such as predictions, content, recommendations, or decisions that can influence environments—and whether it falls into a high-risk category. **EU AI Act Article 3(1).**

High-risk AI systems include systems classified under the AI Act’s high-risk rules, especially systems used in specified areas such as biometrics, education, employment, access to essential services, law enforcement, migration/asylum/border control, administration of justice, and democratic processes. **EU AI Act Article 6 and Annex III.** High-risk systems must meet AI Act controls such as transparency to deployers, technical documentation, accuracy/robustness/cybersecurity, quality management, logging, human oversight, and deployer monitoring/oversight duties. **EU AI Act Articles 11, 13, 14, 15, 17, 26.**

## 2) How they interact in overlap cases

Where a high-risk AI system is used to make a solely automated, consequential decision about a person using personal data—e.g., automated rejection of a loan, automated hiring rejection, automated denial of benefits—**both regimes can apply**.

In that case:

- The AI Act governs the **AI system lifecycle and operator duties**: design controls, documentation, transparency to deployers, human oversight measures, logging, monitoring, and in some cases a fundamental-rights impact assessment. **EU AI Act Articles 11, 13, 14, 15, 17, 26, 27.**
- GDPR Article 22 governs the **individual data-subject right not to be subject to certain solely automated decisions**, plus the legal basis/exceptions and individual safeguards. **GDPR Article 22(1)–(4).**
- GDPR transparency duties may also require meaningful information about automated decision-making, the logic involved, and the significance and envisaged consequences. **GDPR Articles 13(2)(f) and 14(2)(g).**
- GDPR may require a DPIA for systematic and extensive automated evaluation producing legal or similarly significant effects. **GDPR Article 35(3)(a).**
- The AI Act’s fundamental-rights impact assessment can complement an existing GDPR DPIA where obligations overlap. **EU AI Act Article 27(4).**

## 3) Article 22 can apply when the AI Act does not

Yes. Examples:

1. **Automated processing that is not an “AI system.”**  
   GDPR Article 22 applies to decisions based solely on “automated processing,” including profiling. **GDPR Article 22(1).** The AI Act applies to “AI systems” as defined in Article 3(1). **EU AI Act Article 3(1).** A purely deterministic rules engine or simple automated workflow may still be automated processing under GDPR but may not meet the AI Act definition of an AI system.

2. **AI-assisted automated decisions outside AI Act high-risk categories.**  
   Article 22 is sector-neutral: if the decision is solely automated and has legal or similarly significant effects, it can apply. **GDPR Article 22(1).** The AI Act’s high-risk regime applies only where the AI system is classified as high-risk, including under Article 6 and Annex III or relevant product-safety routes. **EU AI Act Article 6 and Annex III.** So a consequential automated decision in a domain not listed as high-risk under the AI Act may still trigger GDPR Article 22.

3. **Systems outside AI Act scope but within GDPR territorial scope.**  
   The GDPR applies to processing by EU-established controllers/processors and, in some cases, non-EU controllers offering goods/services to or monitoring people in the EU. **GDPR Article 3.** The AI Act contains exclusions, including for AI systems used exclusively for military, defence, or national-security purposes, certain scientific R&D systems, pre-market research/testing/development activity, and purely personal non-professional deployer use. **EU AI Act Article 2(3), 2(6), 2(8), 2(10).** Depending on facts, GDPR Article 22 could still be relevant where personal data are processed and the Article 22 threshold is met.

## 4) The AI Act can apply when Article 22 does not

Yes. Examples:

1. **High-risk AI used only as decision support, not solely automated decision-making.**  
   GDPR Article 22 requires a decision “based solely on automated processing.” **GDPR Article 22(1).** If a human makes a genuine, substantive decision using an AI recommendation, Article 22 may not apply, although other GDPR duties may. But the AI Act can still classify the system as high-risk, for example in employment, education, or access to essential services. **EU AI Act Article 6 and Annex III.**

2. **High-risk AI that does not make legal or similarly significant decisions about individuals.**  
   Article 22 requires legal effects or similarly significant effects on a data subject. **GDPR Article 22(1).** The AI Act can apply to high-risk systems based on their intended purpose and risk category, even where the system’s output does not itself constitute a solely automated legal/significant decision. **EU AI Act Article 6 and Annex III.**

3. **High-risk AI not involving personal data.**  
   GDPR applies to processing of personal data. **GDPR Articles 3 and 4.** The AI Act’s definition of AI system is not limited to personal-data processing; it covers machine-based systems generating outputs that influence physical or virtual environments. **EU AI Act Article 3(1).** For example, an AI safety component in a regulated product can be high-risk even if it does not make a personal-data-based decision about a data subject. **EU AI Act Article 6(1) and Annex I.**

4. **Annex III profiling that is high-risk but not Article 22 decision-making.**  
   Under the AI Act, certain Annex III systems may be high-risk, and Annex III systems that perform profiling of natural persons can be treated as high-risk under the AI Act’s classification rules. **EU AI Act Article 6 and Annex III.** But GDPR Article 22 still requires a solely automated decision with legal or similarly significant effects. **GDPR Article 22(1).** Profiling alone is therefore not enough for Article 22 unless it is used for such a decision.

## Bottom line

The overlap is substantial but not complete:

- **GDPR Article 22** asks: *Is there a solely automated personal-data-based decision about an individual with legal or similarly significant effects?* **GDPR Article 22(1).**
- **EU AI Act high-risk status** asks: *Is this an AI system in a high-risk product or use category, or otherwise classified as high-risk under the Act?* **EU AI Act Articles 3(1), 6, Annex I, Annex III.**

So, **Article 22 can apply without the AI Act high-risk regime**, and **the AI Act high-risk regime can apply without Article 22**. Where both apply, the organisation must satisfy both: AI Act system/operator controls and GDPR data-subject protections.

question.question: Compare HIPAA's 'addressable' implementation specifications with SOC 2's flexibility in selecting controls to meet criteria. How do auditors evaluate each?
question.expected_answer: HIPAA's 'addressable' specifications (e.g. §164.312(a)(2)(iv) encryption at rest, §164.312(e)(2)(ii) encryption in transit, §164.308(a)(7)(ii)(D) testing/revision procedures) are not optional: a covered entity must assess whether the spec is reasonable and appropriate; if implemented, do so as written; if not, implement an equivalent alternative AND document the rationale. HHS auditors verify the documented analysis and any alternative measures. SOC 2 is criteria-based: the entity selects controls to meet each Trust Services Criterion; the auditor opines on whether the controls are suitably designed (Type 1) and operating effectively (Type 2). The flexibility is in the choice of controls, not in the criteria themselves. Both regimes allow tailoring but require documentation; HIPAA addressables require explicit justification for non-implementation, SOC 2 requires controls to be present and effective for every criterion in scope.

## Short answer

HIPAA “addressable” specifications are **not optional**; they create a regulated decision process: assess whether the specification is reasonable and appropriate, implement it if so, or document why not and implement an equivalent alternative if reasonable and appropriate. HIPAA cites this expressly at **45 CFR § 164.306(d)(3)**.

SOC 2 is flexible in a different way: the Trust Services Criteria are the evaluation criteria, but management selects and designs controls appropriate to its system, service commitments, system requirements, and risks. SOC 2 “points of focus” are aids, not a mandatory checklist; the AICPA states that use of the criteria “does not require an assessment of whether each point of focus is addressed.” **SOC 2 Trust Services Criteria, Characteristics of the Criteria ¶¶ .05–.07**.

## Comparison

| Topic | HIPAA “addressable” implementation specifications | SOC 2 control-selection flexibility |
|---|---|---|
| Nature of flexibility | Flexibility exists within a legal rule. Covered entities and business associates may use security measures that reasonably and appropriately implement the standards and specifications, considering size, complexity, capabilities, technical infrastructure, cost, and risk to ePHI. **HIPAA, 45 CFR § 164.306(b)(1)–(2)** | Flexibility exists within an attestation framework. Management designs controls to meet applicable Trust Services Criteria based on the entity’s system, service commitments, system requirements, and risks. **SOC 2 Trust Services Criteria, Background ¶ .01; Description Criteria guidance, p. 11** |
| Are listed items optional? | No. “Addressable” means the organization must assess the specification; if reasonable and appropriate, it must implement it. If not, it must document why and implement an equivalent alternative measure if reasonable and appropriate. **HIPAA, 45 CFR § 164.306(d)(3)(i)–(ii)** | Points of focus are not individually required. Some may be irrelevant, management may customize them, and management/practitioners may identify other relevant characteristics. **SOC 2 Trust Services Criteria, Characteristics of the Criteria ¶¶ .05–.07** |
| Baseline obligation | The HIPAA Security Rule standards still apply to all ePHI; the organization must ensure confidentiality, integrity, and availability of ePHI and protect against reasonably anticipated threats and impermissible uses/disclosures. **HIPAA, 45 CFR § 164.306(a), (c)** | The service auditor evaluates whether controls are suitably designed, and for Type 2, operating effectively, to provide reasonable assurance that service commitments and system requirements were achieved based on the applicable Trust Services Criteria. **SOC 2 Trust Services Criteria, p. 3 ¶ .03** |
| Examples | Automatic logoff and encryption/decryption under access control are addressable, but the entity must still go through the § 164.306(d)(3) assessment and documentation process. **HIPAA, 45 CFR § 164.312(a)(2)(iii)–(iv); § 164.306(d)(3)** | A SOC 2 entity may choose different control activities to satisfy criteria such as logical and physical access controls, system operations, change management, or risk mitigation, depending on the scoped system and commitments. **SOC 2 Trust Services Criteria, Organization of the Trust Services Criteria ¶ .08** |

## How auditors or examiners evaluate each

### HIPAA

For HIPAA, an evaluator looks for both **substantive protection** and the **required addressable-specification decision trail**.

Auditors or regulators would typically evaluate whether the covered entity or business associate:

1. **Performed the required assessment** for each addressable specification: whether the safeguard is reasonable and appropriate in its environment, considering its likely contribution to protecting ePHI. **HIPAA, 45 CFR § 164.306(d)(3)(i)**  
2. **Implemented the addressable specification** if it was reasonable and appropriate. **HIPAA, 45 CFR § 164.306(d)(3)(ii)(A)**  
3. If not implemented, **documented why implementation was not reasonable and appropriate** and implemented an equivalent alternative measure if reasonable and appropriate. **HIPAA, 45 CFR § 164.306(d)(3)(ii)(B)**  
4. Considered the rule’s flexibility factors: size, complexity, capabilities, technical infrastructure, cost, and probability/criticality of risks to ePHI. **HIPAA, 45 CFR § 164.306(b)(2)**  
5. Maintained and updated security measures as needed to continue reasonable and appropriate protection of ePHI. **HIPAA, 45 CFR § 164.306(e)**  
6. Maintained records and documentation available for compliance review; HHS may require records and reports and may access books, records, facilities, and other information relevant to compliance. **HIPAA, 45 CFR § 160.310(a)–(c)**  

So, under HIPAA, an auditor does **not** accept “addressable means we skipped it.” The auditor expects a reasoned risk-based determination, documentation, and either implementation or a defensible alternative. **HIPAA, 45 CFR § 164.306(d)(3)**.

### SOC 2

For SOC 2, the CPA service auditor does not audit against a fixed list of prescribed controls. The auditor evaluates whether management’s selected controls, in context, satisfy the applicable Trust Services Criteria.

The SOC 2 auditor evaluates:

1. Whether the system description is fairly presented under the description criteria. **SOC 2 Trust Services Criteria, p. 3 ¶ .03(a); p. 4 ¶ .07**  
2. Whether controls were **suitably designed** to provide reasonable assurance that service commitments and system requirements would be achieved based on the applicable Trust Services Criteria. **SOC 2 Trust Services Criteria, p. 3 ¶ .03(b)**  
3. For a Type 2 report, whether controls **operated effectively** over the review period to provide reasonable assurance that those commitments and requirements were achieved. **SOC 2 Trust Services Criteria, p. 3 ¶ .03(c)**  
4. Whether controls are responsive to the entity’s actual risks, service commitments, system requirements, and selected trust services categories. **SOC 2 Trust Services Criteria, Background ¶¶ .01–.02; Description Criteria guidance, p. 11**  
5. Whether the system description avoids unsupported or inaccurate claims, such as stating that controls exist when they do not or including statements that cannot be objectively evaluated. **SOC 2 Trust Services Criteria, p. 6 ¶ .13**  

Because SOC 2 points of focus are not mandatory, an auditor generally does not issue an exception merely because a particular point of focus was not addressed. Instead, the auditor asks whether the overall set of controls provides reasonable assurance that the applicable criteria are met. **SOC 2 Trust Services Criteria, Characteristics of the Criteria ¶¶ .05–.07; p. 3 ¶ .03**.

## Key distinction

HIPAA addressability is **regulatory flexibility with mandatory analysis and documentation**. SOC 2 flexibility is **control-design flexibility within an attestation against criteria**.

In practice:

- A HIPAA auditor asks: “For this addressable specification, did you assess it, implement it or document why not, and adopt an equivalent alternative if appropriate?” **HIPAA, 45 CFR § 164.306(d)(3)**  
- A SOC 2 auditor asks: “Do the controls management selected, as designed and operated, provide reasonable assurance that the applicable Trust Services Criteria, service commitments, and system requirements are achieved?” **SOC 2 Trust Services Criteria, p. 3 ¶ .03**.

§ 164.306 Security standards: General rules.
  --------------------------------------------

(a) General requirements. Covered entities and business associates must do the following:

(1) Ensure the confidentiality, integrity, and availability of all electronic protected health information the covered entity or business associate creates, receives, maintains, or transmits.

(2) Protect against any reasonably anticipated threats or hazards to the security or integrity of such information.

(4) Ensure compliance with this subpart by its workforce.

(b) Flexibility of approach. (1) Covered entities and business associates may use any security measures that allow the covered entity or business associate to reasonably and appropriately implement the standards and implementation specifications as specified in this subpart.

(2) In deciding which security measures to use, a covered entity or business associate must take into account the following factors:

(i) The size, complexity, and capabilities of the covered entity or business associate.

(ii) The covered entity's or the business associate's technical infrastructure, hardware, and software security capabilities.

(iii) The costs of security measures.

(iv) The probability and criticality of potential risks to electronic protected health information.

(c) Standards. A covered entity or business associate must comply with the applicable standards as provided in this section and in §§ 164.308, 164.310, 164.312, 164.314 and 164.316 with respect to all electronic protected health information.

    A covered entity or business associate must, in accordance with § 164.306:

    (a)(1) Standard: Access control. Implement technical policies and procedures for electronic information systems that maintain electronic protected health information to allow access only to those persons or software programs that have been granted access rights as specified in § 164.308(a)(4).

    (2) Implementation specifications:

    (i) Unique user identification (Required). Assign a unique name and/or number for identifying and tracking user identity.

    (ii) Emergency access procedure (Required). Establish (and implement as needed) procedures for obtaining necessary electronic protected health information during an emergency.

    (iii) Automatic logoff (Addressable). Implement electronic procedures that terminate an electronic session after a predetermined time of inactivity.

    (iv) Encryption and decryption (Addressable). Implement a mechanism to encrypt and decrypt electronic protected health information.

    (b) Standard: Audit controls. Implement hardware, software, and/or procedural mechanisms that record and examine activity in information systems that contain or use electronic protected health information.

    (c)(1) Standard: Integrity. Implement policies and procedures to protect electronic protected health information from improper alteration or destruction.

    (2) Implementation specification: Mechanism to authenticate electronic protected health information (Addressable). Implement electronic mechanisms to corroborate that electronic protected health information has not been altered or destroyed in an unauthorized manner.

    (d) Standard: Person or entity authentication. Implement procedures to verify that a person or entity seeking access to electronic protected health information is the one claimed.

    (e)(1) Standard: Transmission security. Implement technical security measures to guard against unauthorized access to electronic protected health information that is being transmitted over an electronic communications network.

    (2) Implementation specifications:

    (i) Integrity controls (Addressable). Implement security measures to ensure that electronically transmitted electronic protected health information is not improperly modified without detection until disposed of.

    (ii) Encryption (Addressable). Implement a mechanism to encrypt electronic protected health information whenever deemed appropriate.

question.question: Compare NIST AI RMF's GOVERN function with SOC 2's CC1 control environment criteria. What organisational expectations do they share, and what's unique to each?
question.expected_answer: NIST AI RMF GOVERN (sub-categories 1–6) covers AI-specific policies/processes, accountability structures, workforce diversity/competence, engagement with affected communities, AI actor engagement, and third-party AI risk. SOC 2 CC1.1–CC1.5 cover the broader control environment: commitment to integrity and ethical values, board independence and oversight, organisational structures and reporting lines, attracting/developing/retaining competent individuals, and individual accountability. Shared: both require accountability structures, competent personnel, and policy frameworks. Unique to GOVERN: explicit treatment of AI-specific risks (bias, automation harms), engagement with affected communities/stakeholders beyond customers, and AI-actor (developer/deployer/user) role clarity. Unique to CC1: explicit board independence requirement and broader enterprise scope.
question.notes: AI-specific governance vs general control environment.

output.answer:
Below is a comparison of **NIST AI RMF 1.0 — GOVERN** and **SOC 2 — Common Criteria CC1: Control Environment**.

| Area | Shared organisational expectation | NIST AI RMF GOVERN | SOC 2 CC1 Control Environment |
|---|---|---|---|
| Tone from leadership | Both expect senior leadership/governance bodies to set expectations and shape organisational culture. | GOVERN states that governing authorities determine policies directing mission, goals, values, culture, and risk tolerance, and that senior leadership sets the tone for AI risk management. **[NIST AI RMF 1.0, GOVERN, §5.1 / p.22]** | CC1.1 requires the board and management to demonstrate the importance of integrity and ethical values through directives, actions, and behavior. **[SOC 2, CC1.1]** |
| Policies and procedures | Both require organisational policies, processes, and procedures that define expected conduct and risk/control practices. | GOVERN 1 requires AI-risk-related policies, processes, procedures, and practices to be in place, transparent, and effectively implemented. **[NIST AI RMF 1.0, GOVERN 1]** | CC1.1 requires standards of conduct to be defined and understood; CC1.4 requires policies and practices reflecting competence expectations. **[SOC 2, CC1.1; CC1.4]** |
| Roles, responsibilities, and reporting lines | Both require clear assignment of responsibility and communication channels. | GOVERN 2.1 requires roles, responsibilities, and lines of communication for mapping, measuring, and managing AI risks to be documented and clear. **[NIST AI RMF 1.0, GOVERN 2.1]** | CC1.3 requires management, with board oversight, to establish structures, reporting lines, authorities, and responsibilities. **[SOC 2, CC1.3]** |
| Accountability | Both expect mechanisms to hold individuals or teams accountable for risk/control responsibilities. | GOVERN 2 requires accountability structures so appropriate teams and individuals are empowered, responsible, and trained for AI risk management; GOVERN 2.3 assigns executive leadership responsibility for AI system development and deployment risk decisions. **[NIST AI RMF 1.0, GOVERN 2; GOVERN 2.3]** | CC1.5 requires the entity to hold individuals accountable for internal-control responsibilities, including performance measures, incentives, corrective action, rewards, or discipline. **[SOC 2, CC1.5]** |
| Competence and training | Both expect personnel to have the competence and training needed to perform their responsibilities. | GOVERN 2.2 requires personnel and partners to receive AI risk management training consistent with policies, procedures, and agreements. **[NIST AI RMF 1.0, GOVERN 2.2]** | CC1.4 requires the entity to attract, develop, and retain competent individuals, evaluate competence, address shortcomings, and provide training to maintain technical competency. **[SOC 2, CC1.4]** |
| Third parties / partners | Both include expectations for external parties, though framed differently. | GOVERN 2.2 extends AI risk management training expectations to partners. **[NIST AI RMF 1.0, GOVERN 2.2]** | CC1.1 considers contractors and vendor employees in standards of conduct; CC1.3 considers interactions with external parties; CC1.4 evaluates competence of outsourced service providers, contractors, and vendor employees. **[SOC 2, CC1.1; CC1.3; CC1.4]** |

## What they share

They share a common governance foundation: leadership commitment, clear structures, defined responsibilities, competent personnel, accountability mechanisms, and policies that translate organisational values into day-to-day risk/control practices. NIST frames these expectations around **AI risk management across the AI lifecycle**, while SOC 2 frames them around the **internal control environment supporting service commitments and system requirements**. **[NIST AI RMF 1.0, GOVERN §5.1; SOC 2, CC1.1–CC1.5]**

## What is unique to NIST AI RMF GOVERN

NIST AI RMF GOVERN is uniquely AI-specific. It requires governance to support the mapping, measuring, and managing of **AI risks**, including risks to users and broader society. **[NIST AI RMF 1.0, GOVERN §5.1]**

It explicitly integrates the characteristics of **trustworthy AI** into organisational policies, processes, procedures, and practices. **[NIST AI RMF 1.0, GOVERN 1.2]**

It requires AI legal and regulatory requirements to be understood, managed, and documented. **[NIST AI RMF 1.0, GOVERN 1.1]**

It addresses the full AI system lifecycle, including inventorying AI systems and safely decommissioning or phasing them out. **[NIST AI RMF 1.0, GOVERN 1.6; GOVERN 1.7]**

It uniquely prioritises diversity, equity, inclusion, and accessibility in AI risk decision-making, including diverse teams and defined roles for human-AI oversight configurations. **[NIST AI RMF 1.0, GOVERN 3.1; GOVERN 3.2]**

It requires a “critical thinking and safety-first mindset” in the design, development, deployment, and use of AI systems to reduce potential negative impacts. **[NIST AI RMF 1.0, GOVERN 4.1]**

## What is unique to SOC 2 CC1

SOC 2 CC1 is uniquely grounded in the **COSO control environment** and focuses on whether the organisation’s internal control environment supports the achievement of service commitments and system requirements. **[SOC 2, Organisation of Trust Services Criteria, p.5; SOC 2, Description Criteria ¶.07]**

SOC 2 CC1 explicitly requires the board to demonstrate independence from management and exercise oversight over the development and performance of internal control. **[SOC 2, CC1.2]**

SOC 2 CC1 places more detailed emphasis on integrity and ethical values, including standards of conduct, evaluation of adherence, and timely remediation of deviations. **[SOC 2, CC1.1]**

SOC 2 CC1 is more prescriptive about organisational structure, reporting lines, authority limits, segregation of duties, and governance of external-party interactions in support of security, availability, processing integrity, confidentiality, and privacy objectives. **[SOC 2, CC1.3]**

SOC 2 CC1 gives more detailed criteria for workforce competence, including background considerations, technical competency, succession planning, and continuing education. **[SOC 2, CC1.4]**

SOC 2 CC1 also more explicitly ties accountability to performance measures, incentives, rewards, excessive pressure, discipline, and corrective action. **[SOC 2, CC1.5]**

## Bottom line

The overlap is strongest at the level of **enterprise governance discipline**: leadership tone, clear accountability, documented responsibilities, competent people, training, and policies that make risk/control expectations operational. The difference is that **NIST AI RMF GOVERN is an AI-risk governance model**, with lifecycle, trustworthy-AI, societal-impact, human-oversight, and AI inventory/decommissioning expectations; **SOC 2 CC1 is an internal-control environment model**, with stronger emphasis on board independence, ethical conduct, control accountability, competence, and service-system assurance.
